Stress arises less from specific events & more from how we appraise those events

- Comes from catastrophes, significant life changes, & daily hassles  
- Appraise as a challenge or threat? Decision determines whether become stressed to distraction or aroused & motivated

Women have higher stress than men

Teens & early twenties report feeling stressed \~50% of the day

Conflict

- **Approach approach** – must choose between two desirable outcomes  
- **Avoidance avoidance** – must choose between two undesirable outcomes  
- **Approach avoidance**  
- **Multiple approach avoidance** – choose between some outcomes that are good and some that are bad

**Han Selye** named stress response: **General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)**

- 3 stages:   
  - Alarm  
  - Resistance  
  - Exhaustion

**Tend-and-befriend** \- theory that when under stress, people will often provide support to others and bond with and seek support from others (women especially do this)

![][image1]

Stress can make you more susceptible to illness

Psychophysiological illness \- “mind-body” illness; stress related illness that effects both mind and body

Psychoneuroimmunology \- the study of how psychoneural things effect our health

Lymphocytes \- two types of white blood cells that are part of immune system

- B \- bacterial infection fighters  
- T \- attacks foreign substances, viruses, & cancer cells  
- Macrophage \- fights other harmful intruders like worn-out cells needing to be cleaned up  
- Natural killer cells \- fights diseased cells affected by viruses or cancer

Prolonged stress like severe childhood stress can damage the body

- Shortened telomeres were found in those who experienced severe childhood stress  
- Causes premature aging  
- Increases disease risk

Stress leads to a faster decline in sick people with things like cancer & AIDS

Stress is directly related to Heart Disease (leading cause of death in North Americans)

**Coronary Heart Disease** \- clogs vessels in the heart

**Type A person** \- competitive, hard-driven

**Tybe B** \- easygoing, relaxed

Pessimists are more likely to develop heart disease than optimists

Chronic stressors lead to excessive inflamation, which can cause depressive symptoms & cardiac disease

**Adaptation-level phenomenon** \- tendency to form judgements relative to a neutral level defined by prior experience

**Relative deprivation**

**Positive Psychology** \- the study of human flourishing

**Subjective well-being** \- your perception of being happy or satisfied with life

- Relative

Feel-good do-good phenomenon

Optimists have a stronger immune system, more stable blood pressure, fast recovery from surgery, and longer lifespan

**ADHD** \- innatention, hyperactivity, impulsivity

- Neurodevelopmental disorder  
- Diagnosed often in early childhood, usually shows up before age 12  
  - Academic difficulties, organization, memory, & social challenges, executive functioning issues  
- Increased risk of academic issues, low self-esteem, & risk taking  
- Most diagnosed people will continue to see issues into adulthood  
- Academic issues, social functioning impairment  
  


**Generalized Anxiety disorder**

- Excessive, uncontrollable worry  
- Autonomic nervous system aroused without pinpointable reason  
- Can develop gradually, often begins late adolescence/early adulthood  
- Lead to sleep deprivation, decreased performance, manifest physically

**Phobia**

- Consistent and irrational fear about something specific  
- Often begins in childhood  
- Sometimes resolves naturally

**OCD** (review in notes as well)

- time consuming and distressing compulsions  
- Onset in adolescence or early adulthood  
- Can create work and family relationships issues 

**PTSD**

- Nightmares and haunting memories  
- Trauma-related stimuli  
- Social withdrawal, anxiety, numbness  
- Diagnosed when symptoms linger for 4 weeks or more after trauma

**Dissociative amnesia** with fugue state

- Inability to recall important autobiographical info  
- Usually related to traumatic event  
- Memory loss that’s more extensive than just “I forgot”

**Fugue state** \= an unexpected occurrence of dissociative amnesia

- May appear normal during this time  
- Some amnesia is common and ongoing after end of fugue state  
- Linked to trauma  
- Emotional numbness & confusion  
- Onset happens at any age, more common early adulthood  
- Can be brief amnesia episodes or longer like weeks or months

DID

- Multiple distinct identities or personalities  
- Onset strongly associated with severe childhood trauma, especially physical or sexual abuse  
- Symptoms often begin in childhood, but not diagnosed until later  
- Trouble maintaining consistent performance, high levels of distress  
- Common co-occuring conditions are depression & anxiety  
- Multiple personality

1) Research method  
2) Operational definition of risky behavior  
3) Describe meanings of the differences in means for the groups that were excluded and the groups that were included in their preference for risky behavior  
4) ID one ethical guideline  
5) Generalizability  
6) Explain how findings support/refute hypothesis

1\)	Researchers in this study did an experiment used an experimental method to test the effect of social exclusion on risky behavior. 

2\) as measured on a 1:8 scale (stronger to riskier) → connect lottery scale to riskier choice, identify correlation

3\) tell mean of excluded group and compare to that of included group → significance

4\) ethical guideline → consent form/informed consent, debriefing

5\) Not generalizable, because participants are limited in ages, socioeconomic backgrounds, etc.

6\) research findings support the hypothesis because there was a strong correlation found between those who experienced those who experienced social exclusion (mean \_\_\_) and riskier financial decisions

| Term | Definition | Significance/examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Critical Thinking | Does not immediately accept arguments & conclusions but examines assumptions, appraises the source, discerns hidden bias, evaluates evidence, & assesses conclusions |  |
| Hindsight Bias | The tendency to believe, after learning an outcome, that one would have foreseen it; the “I knew it all along” phenomenon |  |
| Peer reviewers | Scientific experts who evaluate a research article’s theory, originality, & accuracy |  |
| Theory | An explanation using an integrated set of principles that organizes observations & predicts behaviors or events |  |
| Hypothesis | A testable prediction, often implied by a theory |  |
| Falsifiable | The possibility that an idea, hypothesis, or theory can be disproven by observation or experiment |  |
| Operational Definition | Carefully worded statement of the exact procedures used in a research study |  |
| Replication | Repeating the essence of a research study, usually with different participants in different situations, to see whether the basic finding can be reproduced |  |
| Case study | A non-experimental technique in which one individual or group is studied in depth in the hope of revealing universal principles |  |
| Naturalistic observation | A non-experimental technique of observing & recording behavior in naturally occurring situations without trying to manipulate and control a situation |  |
| survey | Non-experimental technique for obtaining the self-reported attitudes & behaviors of a particular group, usually by questioning a representative, *random sample* of the group |  |
| Social desirability bias | From others’ responding in ways that they presume a researcher expects or wishes |  |
| Self-report bias | When people inaccurately report their behavior |  |
| Sampling bias | A flawed sampling process that produces an unrepresentative sample |  |
| Random sample | Sample that fairly represents a population because each member has an equal chance of inclusion |  |
| population | All those in a group being studied, from which random samples may be drawn |  |
| correlation | A measure of the extent to which two factors vary together, and thus of how well either factor predicts the other |  |
| Correlation coefficient | A statistical index of the relationship between two variables (from \-1 to \+1) |  |
| variable | Anything that can vary and is feasible and ethical to measure |  |
| scatterplot | Graphed cluster of dots, each of which represents the values of 2 variables; the slope suggests the direction of the relationship between two variables; the amount of scatter suggests the strength of the correlation |  |
| Illusory correlation | Perceiving a relationship where there is none, or perceiving a stronger-than-actual relationship |  |
| Regression toward the mean | Tendency for extreme or unusual scores or events to fall back (regress) toward the average |  |
| Experimental group | In an experiment, the group exposed to treatment/one version of the independent variable |  |
| experiment | Research method in which the investigator manipulates one or more factors to observe the effect on some behavior or mental process; by random assignment of participants, the experimenter aims to control other relevant factors |  |
| Control group | The group not exposed to the treatment; contrasts with the experimental group and serves as a comparison for evaluating the effect of a treatment |  |
| Random assignment | Assigning participants to the experiment and control groups by chance, thus minimizing preexisting differences between different control groups |  |
| Single blind procedure | Experimental procedure in which research participants are ignorant about whether they have received the treatment or a placebo |  |
| Placebo effect | Experimental results caused by expectation alone; any effect or behavior caused by the administration of an inert substance or condition, which the recipient assumes is an active agent |  |
| Independent variable | In an experiment, the factor that is manipulated, the variable whose effect is being studied |  |
| Confounding variable | In an experiment, a factor other than the factor being studied that might influence a study’s results |  |
| Experimenter bias | Bias caused when researchers may unintentionally influence results to confirm their own beliefs |  |
| Dependent variable | In an experiment, the outcome that is measured; the variable that may change when the independent variable is manipulated |  |
| validity | The extent to which a test or experiment measures or predicts what it is supposed to |  |
| Qualitative research | A research method that relies on in-depth, narrative data that are not translated into numbers |  |
| Quantitative data | Research method that relies on quantifiable, numerical data |  |
| Informed consent | Giving potential participants enough information about a study to enable them to choose whether they wish to participate |  |
| debriefing | The post-experimental explanation of a study, including its purpose and any deceptions, to its participants |  |
| Double-blind procedure | An experimental procedure in which both the research participants and research staff are ignorant about whether the research participants have recieved the treatment or placebo | Commonly used in drug evaluation studies |
| Descriptive statistics | Numerical data used to measure or describe characteristics of groups; includes measures of central tendency & measures of variation |  |
| histogram | Bar graph depicting a frequency distribution | ![][image17] |
| mode | The most frequently occuring scores in a distribution |  |
| mean | Arithmetic average of a distribution, obtained by adding scores and then dividing by the number of scores |  |
| median | The middle score in a distribution; half the scores are above it, half are below it |  |
| Percentile rank | Percentage of scores lower than a given score |  |
| Skewed distribution | Representation of scores that lack symmetry around their average value |  |
| range | The difference between the highest and lowest scores in a distribution |  |
| Standard deviation | A computed measure of how much scores vary around the mean score |  |
| Normal curve | A symmetrical, bell shaped curve that describes the distribution of many types of data; most scores fall near the mean & fewer scores lie near the extremes; AKA normal distribution |  |
| Generalize | To infer from sample data the probability of something being true for a population |  |
| meta-analysis | Statistical procedure for analyzing results of multiple studies to reach an overall conclusion |  |
| Statistical significance | A statistical statement of how likely it is that a result (such as a difference between samples) occurred by chance, assuming there is no difference between the populations being studied |  |
| Effect size | Strength of a relationship between the two variables; the larger effect size, the more one variable can be explained by the other |  |
| Experimental research |  |  |
| Correlational research |  |  |
| Observational research |  |  |
| Meta analysis research |  |  |

Twins are ideal subjects of studies on Nature v. nurture

Charles Darwin, *Origin of species*, and natural selection theory

Interaction between environment and heredity  
Bio-psycho-social creatures → combination of nature and nurture

- **Heredity** \= genetics, etc.  
- **Nurture** \= home, prenatal care, etc. 

Our genetic predispositions and our surrounding environments interact. Environments can trigger gene activity, and genetically influenced traits can evoke responses from others. 

**Natural selection**

- Every species contains variation, and individuals best adapted to the environment survive; survival of the fittest  
- The evolutionary perspective explores how natural selection affects the expression of behavior and mental processes to increase survival and reproductive success  
- evolutionary perspective is the purview of psychological scientists who study the role of natural selection in the evolution of psychological mechanisms that allow adaptation to recurring behavioral problems (e.g., avoiding toxic foods, mate selection, altruism, social competition) relevant to species survival.

**Eugenics** \- Some theorists have sought to apply principles of the evolutionary perspective in ways that discriminate against others (eugenics); the pseudoscientific view that the genetic makeup of the population can be improved by selective breeding and by preventing reproduction by people with various disabilities

- Nazis adapted to their own aims in formulating the “final solution” in World War II

- **Twin studies** \- study diff. Types of twins to determine personality similarity  
- **Family studies** \- parenting has little effect on the way children behave   
  - Applies only to ordinary families (not abusive households, etc.)  
- **Adoption studies**

- work because they either increase or mirror neurotransmitters (**agonists**) or block receptor sites (**antagonists**)

**Reuptake inhibitors** block the reuptake process, leaving the **drug**/ **neurotransmitter** in the synaptic gap longer

**BRAIN STRUCTURE**  
Two brain hemispheres: left and right

- Connected by neural fibers called corpus callosum  
- Each side controls the opposite side of the body

4 different lobes in each hemisphere (brain hat)

- Temporal lobe  
- Frontal lobe  
- Occipital lobe  
- Parital lobe

Cerebral cortex \- wrinkly covering of brain → ultimate control center

- Wrinkles allow for more surface area and neural connections

Cerebellum \- baby brain; coordinates voluntary movements, balance, learning, and memories

Amygdala \- controls fear, agression; linked to emotion

Hippocampus \- memory

**Hypothalamus** \- temperature, eating, emotion

- Medulla  
- pituitary gland \- endocrine system  
- Pons \- bulge structure in brain stem; coordinate movement  
- Recticular formation \- arousal  
  * Won’t wake up without it  
- Thalamus \- responsible for movement of sensory information

- Since we listen to music, the **temporal lobe** is used for hearing audio → part of **auditory cortex**  
- Parrots are colorful, loud, and smelly things that **paretial lobe** processes  
- **Cerebellum** \- Ceraballerina → balance  
- **Hypothalamus** → temperature regulation and thirst (hypothermia)

Consciousness

- Various states of consciousness: awake, sleeping, etc.   
- Can be influenced by drugs

Brain scans of unresponsive patients show that there is still awareness and brain activity if a person is not awake

We are aware of what is within the limited spotlight of consciousness, but much information is processed simultaneously in the unconscious mind

- This duality is sometimes referred to as “**high road-consciousness**” and “**low road-unconsciousness**”.   
  Together, tracks provide integrated functioning in a process known as dual processing.

Beginning of sleep sycle – **Beta waves**

**Alpha waves** – between sleep and wakefulness

**Theta waves** \- when someone crosses into stage one (light) sleep

- Hypnic jerks can occur

**Sleep spindles and K complexities** 

**Delta waves** \- deep sleep, completely unaware of most

**REM** \- dreaming, brain activity resembles being awake \- final sleep stage

- REMember your dreams  
- REMain still → associated with muscle paralysis

Sleep is the periodic loss of consciousness → still have some level of awareness

- For protection, recuperation, growth, memory

NREM 

1) Light sleep, easily woken  
   1) Can experience hallucinations (false sensory experiences) – and hypnagogic sensations (bizarre experiences such as jerking with a sensation of falling)  
2) Fully asleep → theta waves with sleep spindles (random short bursts of activity that help in memory processing) & k-complexities (random tall bursts of activity about 20 min)   
   1) Fairly easy to be woken  
3) Deep sleep → deltawaves (30min), hard to wake

REM: body relaxed as if paralyzed but brain as active as if it was awake (paradoxical sleep) → BETA waves

Increased sleep associated with better grades, less depression, better moods

Sleep deprivation increses hunger, impacts weight, messes with horomones and metabolism, increases risk for heart disease and other negative health outcomes, slows reaction time, less focus, lower immune response, reduced strengths, increase in hunger, decreased ability to process and store memories

| Term | Definition | Significance/examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Nature v. nurture** | The longstanding controversy over the relatice contributions that genes and experience make to the development of psychological traits and behaviors | Today we believe that a combination of the two lead to the development of traits and behaviors |
| **Charles Darwin** | Wrote *On the Origin of Species*; explained diversity by proposing natural selection |  |
| **Natural Selection** | Survival of the fittest; the principle that the inherited traits enabling an organism to survive and reproduce in a particular environment will most likely be passed on to succeeding generations | Finches with diff. Beaks on the island |
| **Twin Studies** | Assess effects of shared genes | Bogata Brothers |
| **Family studies** | Search for traits and diseases that tend to be shared by family members |  |
| **Adoption Studies** | Assess effects of shared environments |  |
| **Evolutionary psychology** | The study of the evolution of behavior and the mind, using principles of natural selection |  |
| **Behavior genetics** | The study of the relative power and limits of genetic and environmental influences and behavior |  |
| **mutations** | A random error in gene replication that leads to a change |  |
| **environment** | Every nongenetic influence, from prenatal nutrition to our experiences of the people and things around us |  |
| **heredity** | The genetic transfer of characteristics from parents to offspring | Sydney Sweeney has great jeans |
| **genes** | The biochemical units of heredity | Codes for our life |
| **genome** | The complete instructions for making an organism | What makes the difference between humans and bananas |
| **Identical (monozygotic) twins** | Individuals who developed from a single fertilized egg that split into two, creating two genetically identical organisms | Bogata brothers |
| **Fraternal (dizygotic) twins** | Individuals who developed from separate fertilized eggs; are genetically no closer than ordinary siblings, but shared a prenatal environment |  |
| **interaction** | The interplay that occurs when the effect of one factor (like environment) depends on another factor (like heredity) |  |
| **Epigenetics** | “Above” or “in addition to” genetics: the study of the molecular mechanisms by which environments can influence genetic expression (without a DNA change) | The things in DNA that are changeable; written in pencil |
| **Nervous system** | The body’s speedy, electrochemical communication network consisting of all the nerce cells of the peripheral and central nervous systems |  |
| **Central nervous system** | The brain & spinal cord |  |
| **Peripheral nervous system** | The sensory and motor neurons that connect the central nervous system to the rest of the body |  |
| **nerves** | Bundlesd axons that form neural cables connecting the central nercous system with muscles, glands, and sensory organs |  |
| **Sensory (afferent) neurons** | Neurons that carry incoming info. From the body’s tissues and sensory receptors to the brain and spinal cord |  |
| **Motor (efferent) neurons** | Neurons that carry outgoing info. From the brain and spinal cord to the uscles and glands |  |
| **interneurons** | Neurons within the brain and spinal cord; they communicate internally and process info. Between the sensory inputs and motor outputs |  |
| **Somatic nervous system** | Division of the peripheral nervous system that constols the body’s skeletal muscles (skeletal nervous system) |  |
| **Autonomic nervous system** | The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls the glands and muscles of internal organs; sympathetic division arouses; parasympathetic division calms |  |
| **Sympathetic nervous system** | The division of the autonomic nervous system that arouses the body, mobilizing its energy in stressful situations |  |
| **Parasympathetic nervous system** | The division of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body, conserving its energy |  |
| **reflex** | A simple, automatic response to a sensory stimulus | Knee-jerk reflex |
| **neuron** | A nerve cell; the basic building block of the nervous system |  |
| **Cell body** | The part of a neuron that contains the nucleus; the cell’s life support center |  |
| **dendrites** | Neuron’s bushy, branching extensions that receive messages and conduct impulses toward the cell body |  |
| **axon** | The neuron extension that passes messages through its branches to other neurons or to muscles or glands |  |
| **Myelin sheath** | A layer of fatty tissue segmentally encasint the axons of some neurons; enables vastly greater transmission speed as neural impulses hop from one node to the next |  |
| **Glial cells** | Cells in the nervous system that support, nourish, and protect neurons; they may also play a role in learning, thinking, and memory |  |
| **Action potential** | A neural impulse; a brief electrical charge that travels down an axon |  |
| **threshold** | A level of stimulation required to trigger a neural impulse |  |
| **Refractory period** | A period of inactivity after a neuron has fired |  |
| **All-or-none response** | A neuron’s reaction of either firing (with a full strength response) or not firing |  |
| **synapse** | The junction between the axon tip of the sending neuron and the dendrite or cell body of the recieving neuron; gap at this junction is the synaptic gap |  |
| **neurotransmitters** | Chemical messengers that cross the synaptic gaps between neurons; travel across synapse and bind to receptor sites on recieving neuron, influencing whether that neuron will generate a neural impulse |  |
| **reuptake** | A neurotransmitter’s reabsorbtion by the sending neuron |  |
| **endorphins** | “Morphine within”; natural, opioid-like neurotransmitters linked to perception of pain and pleasure | Undersupply linked to depression, oversupply makes people anxious/wired |
| **agonist** | A molecule that increases a neurotransmitter’s action |  |
| **antagonist** | A molecule that inhibits or blocks a neurotransmitter’s action |  |
| **Endocrine system** | The body’s “slow” chemical communication system; a set of glands and fat tissue that secrete horomones into the bloodstream |  |
| **Horomones** | Chemical messengers that are manufactured by the endocrine glands, travel through the bloodstream, and affect other tissues |  |
| **Acetylcholine** | Enables muscle action, learning, and memory; skeletal muscles; excitatory | Undersupply linked to Alzheimer’s, oversupply linked to paralysis |
| **Dopamine** | Influences voluntary movement, learning, attention, and emotion; excitatory | Oversupply linked to schitzophrenia, undersupply linked to parkinson’s |
| **seratonin** | Affects mood, hunger, sleep, and arousal | Undersupply linked to depression |
| **Norepinephrine** | Helps control alertness and arousal | Undersupply linked to depression Oversupply linked to anxiety/mania |
| **GABA (gammaaminob-utyric acid** | A major inhibitory neurotransmitter | Undersupply linked to seizures, tremors, and insomnia |
| **Glutamate** | A major excitatory neurotransmitter; involved in memory | Undersupply linked to concentration problems, oversupply linked to seizures and migranes |
| **Substance P** | Involved in pain perception and immune response | Oversupply lead to chronic pain |
| **Psychoactive drug** | A chemical substance that alters the brain, causing changes in perceptions and mood |  |
| **Substance use disorder** | A disorder characterized by continued substance use despite resulting in life disruption |  |
| **depressants** | Drugs that reduce neural activity and slow body functions |  |
| **tolerance** | The diminishing effect with regular use of the same dose of a drug, requiring the user to take larger and larger doses before experiencing the drug’s effect |  |
| **addiction** | An everyday term for compulsive substance use (and sometimes for dysfunctional behavior patterns, such as gambling) that continue despite harmful consequences |  |
| **withdrawal** | The discomfort and distress that follow discontinuing an addictive drug or behavior |  |
| **barbituates**  | Drugs that depress central nervous system activity, reducing anxiety but impairing memory and judgement |  |
| **opioids** | Opium and its derivatives; they depress neural activity, temporariy lessening pain and anxiety |  |
| **stimulants** |  Drugs that excite neural activity and speed up bodily functions |  |
| **hallucinogens** | Psychedelic drugs that distort perceptions and evoke sensory images in the absence of sensory imput |  |
| **Near-death experience** | An altered state of consciousness reported after a close brush with death; often similar to drug-induced hallucinations |  |
| **Electroencephalogram (EEG)** | Amplified recording of the waves of the brain’s electrical activity (“brainwaves”) sweeping across the brain’s surface measured via electrodes placed on scalp | Low resolution; non-invasive |
| **Computerized Axial Tomography (CAT, CT)** | A series of X-ray photos taken from different angles and combined by computer into a composite representation of a slice of the brain’s structure | High resolution imaging of brain structure; potential damage because of high radiation levels |
| **Positron Emmission Tomography (PET)** | Displays where a radioactive form of glucose goes while the brain performs a given task | Which brain areas consume most energy in a given task; brain function; radiation injection; long process & expensive |
| **Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)** | A technique that uses magnetic fields and radio waves to produce computer-generated images of soft tissue; MRI scans show brain anatomy | Uncomfortable for claustrophobia; no info about brain function; examine brain structure without radiation exposure |
| **Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI)** | Type of MRI that detects amount of bloodflow in different brain regions and therefore brain activity by comparing successive MRI scans; shows brain structure and function | Quick, uncomfortable for clostrophobia |
| **MEG (magrnetoencephalography)** | A brain-imaging technique that measures magnetic fields from the brain’s natural electrical activity |  |
| **Biological psychology** | The study of the links between biological (genetic, neural, horomonal) processes; also called behavioral neuroscientists, neuropsychologists, behavior geneticists, or biopsychologists |  |
| **Biosychosial approach** | Integrated approach that incorporates biological, psycological, and socio-cultural levels of analysis |  |
| **Levels of analysis** | The differing complementary veiws, from Biological to psychological to socio-cultural, analyzing any given phenomenon |  |
| **neuroplasticity** | The brain’s ability to change, especially during childhood, by reorganizing after damage or building new pathways based on experience |  |
| **leison** | Tissue destruction; may occur naturally, during surgery, or experimentally |  |
| **hindbrain** | Consists of the medulla, pons, and cerebellum; directs essential survival functions, such as breathing, sleeping, arousal, and coordination and balance |  |
| **midbrain** | Found atop the brainstem, connects the hindbrain with the forebrain, controls some motor movement, and transmits auditory and visual information |  |
| **forebrain** | Consists of the thalamus, cerebral cortex, and hypothalamus; manages complex and cognitive activities, sensory and associative functions, and voluntary motor devices |  |
| **Brainstem** | Oldest part of central core of brain, beginning where spinal cord swells as it enters the skill; responsible for automatic survival functions |  |
| **Medulla** | Base of brainstem; controls heartbeat and breathing |  |
| **Thalamus** | Sensory switchboard; on top of brainstem; directs messages to sensory recieving areas in cortex and transmits replies to cerebellum and medulla |  |
| **Recticular formation** | Nerve network that travels through the brainstem and thalamus and plays an important role in conrolling arousal |  |
| **cerebellum** | “Little brain” at rear of brainstem; functions include processing sensory input and coordinating movement output and balance, enabling nonverbal learning and memory |  |
| **Limbic system** | Neural system located mostly in the forebreain – below the cerebral hemispheres— that includes the amygdala, hypothalamus, hippocampus, thalamus, and pituitary gland; associated with emotions and drives |  |
| **amygdala** | Two lima-bean-sized neural clusters in the limbic system; linked to emotion |  |
| **hypothalamus** | The limbic system neural structure lying below the thalamus; directs maintenance activities (eating, drinking, body temp.), helps govern endocrine system and is linked to emotion and reward |  |
| **hippocampus** | A neural center in the limbic system that helps process explicit (conscious) memories of facts and events for storage |  |
| **Cerebral cortex** | Intricate fabric of interconnected neural cells covering the cerebral hemispheres; body’s ultimate control and information processing center |  |
| **Frontal lobes** | Portion of cerebral cortex lying behind forehead; involved in speaking and muscle movements and in making plans and judgements |  |
| **Parietal lobes** | Portion of cerebral cortex lying at the top of the head and toward the rear; recieves sensory input for tough and body position |  |
| **Occipital lobes** | Portion of the cerebral cortex lying at the back of the head; includes areas that receive information from visual fields |  |
| **Temporal lobes** | Portion of cerebral cortex lying roughly above ears; includes auditory areas, each revieving information primarily from opposite ear |  |
| **Motor cortex** | An area at the rear of the frontal lobes that controls voluntary movements |  |
| **somatosensory cortex** | A cerebral cortex area at the front of the parietal lobes that registers and processes body touch and movement sensations |  |
| **Association areas** | Areas of the cerebral cortex that are not involved in primary motor or sensory function, but rather are involved in higher mental functions like learning, remembering, thinking, and speaking |  |
| **neurogenisis** | The formation of new neurons |  |
| **Corpus callosum** | Large band of neural fibers connecting the two brain hemispheres and carrying messages between them |  |
| **Roger Sperry & Michael Gazzaniga** | Neurosurgeons who divided cats’ and monkey’s brains by severing the corpus callosum and studied split brained patients |  |
| **Split brain** | A condition resulting from surgery that separates the brain’s two hemispheres by cutting the fibers connecting them |  |
| **Consciousness** | Our subjective awareness of ourselves and our environment |  |
| **Cognitive neuroscience** | Interdisciplinary study of the brain activity linked with cognition (perception, thinking, memory, and language) |  |
| **Dual processing** | Processing the principle that information is often simultaneously processed on separate conscious and unconscious tracks |  |
| **Blindsight** | a condition in which a person can respond to a visual stimulus without consciously experiencing it |  |
| **Parallel processing** | Processing multiple aspects of a stimulus simultaneously |  |
| **Sequential processing** | Processing one aspect of a stimulus at a time; used to process new information and solve difficult problems |  |
| **Sleep** | A periodic, natural loss of consciousness – as distinct from unconsciousness resulting from a coma, general anesthesia, or hibernation |  |
| **Circadian rythm** | Biological clock that regulates regular bodily rhythms like mood, temperature, and arousal through a 24 hour cycle | Can be thrown by work schedule or time zone change; vary by age and individual → menstrual cycle, mating cycle, etc. |
| **NREM** | Non rapid eye movement sleep; encompasses all sleep stages except for REM sleep |  |
| **REM sleep** | Rapid eye movement sleep; a recurring sleep stage during which vivid dreams commonly occur; also known as paradoxical sleep because muscles are relaxed but other body systems are still active |  |
| **Alpha waves** | The relatively slow brain waves of a relaxed, awake state |  |
| **Delta waves** | The large, slow brain waves associated with deep sleep |  |
| **Hallucinations** | False sensory experiences, such a seeing something in the absence of a visual stimulus |  |
| **Hypnagogic senstations** | Bizarre experiences, such as jerking or a feeling of falling or floating weightlessly, while transitioning into sleep | Also called hypnic sensations |
| **Suprachiasmatic nucleus** | A pair of cell clusters in the hypothalamus that controls circadian rhythm; adjusts melatonin production in response to light, modifying feelings of sleepiness |  |
| **Insomnia** | Recurring problems falling or staying asleep |  |
| **narcolepsy** | A sleep disorder characterized by uncontrollable sleep attacks; sufferer may lapse directly into REM sleep |  |
| **Sleep apnea** | A sleep disorder characterized by temporary cessations of breathing during sleep and repeated momentary wakings |  |
| **REM sleep behavior disorder** | A rare sleep disorder in which the person is not immobilized during REM sleep, physically “acting out” their dream |  |
| **Sigmund Freud** | Wrote *The Interpretation of Dreams*; thought that dreams provided a psychic safety valve that discharges otherwise unacceptable feelings |  |
| **REM rebound** | The tendency for REM sleep to increase following REM sleep deprivation |  |
| **Dreams** | Sequences of images, emotions, and thoughts passing through a sleeping person’s mind; most vivid during REM sleep |  |
| **Info. processing/ Memory consolidation theory** | Dreams are the expression of a person’s thoughts/experiences, allowing them to convert necessary information into long-term memory |  |
| **Activation synthesis theory** | Dreams are merely the result of our brain trying to synthesize random neural activity during sleep, which our brain crafts into a narrative; neural activity triggered that evokes random visual memories that our brain weaves into stories | Developed by Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley; why dreams sometimes make no sense |

Sensation and perception  
Use prior knowledge for top-down processing

Bottom up and top down processing work together 

Perception is influenced by whether one primarily relies on 

Must hit absolute threshold to consciously be aware of neural impulses 50% of the time

- There is no uniform absolute threshold  
- Other species can see and hear at different frequencies

Signal detection theory 

- How people respond to stimuli and reactions change over time

Wavelengths & amplitude → see chem notes

Childhood development  
Jean Piaget \- developmental psychologist

- Created stages of cognitive development  
- Believed that children are active thinkers

**Schema**, **Assimilation, accommodation**

[**Piaget stage rap**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iTzVWX1Ahg4) 

Piaget said there were 4 stages:

1) **sensorimotor stage**  
   1) **Object permanence** → peekaboo  
   2) Baby physics  
   3) Baby math  
2) **Preoporational stage**  
   1) 6-7 years old  
   2) Represent things with words and images  
   3) **Conservation** → understanding conservation of math  
      1) This age can’t comprehend the conservation of mass  
      2) Tall glass vs. short glass example  
   4) **Egocentric** \- self-focused  
   5) Have trouble with **theory of mind** → have trouble comprehending feelings of others   
      1) Red vs. blue cupboard ball example  
3) \_\_\_\_ stage  
4) \_\_\_\_\_ stage

**Influential theory**

- Development is more continuous than Piaget thought  
- Larger emphasis on social factors

**Lev Vygotsky’s Scaffolding**

- Saw kids as mini apprentices  
- Stressed the importance of social interaction  
- The idea of progressing along the “scaffolding” of development levels  
- Child can learn with or without help  
- **Zone of proximal development**  
  


  
Lawrence Kohlberg focuses on moral development

- Preconventional morality \- prior to age 9, morality focused on self-interest  
- Conventional morality \- by early adolescence; morality is focused on caring for others and upholding social rules… “just because”  
- Postconventional morality \- with the abstract reasoning of formal operational thought, this level may be reached…apply personal rights to a sense of moral right and wrong → going against unjust laws

Moral intuition, moral action

# Sex & Gender

Sex v. Gender

- Intersex   
- Female  
- Male 

Males tend to be more aggressive, especially physically  
Females are more likely to be psychologically aggressive

Males tend to be more skilled at math  
Females tend to be smarter linguistically and emotionally

Girls more likely to start period early bc of outside factors

1. Mother smoked during pregnancy  
2. Sexual abuse

Sex orientation is not willfully chosen or willfully changed

- Some genetic influence has been hypothesized & shown in twin studies
